items.title: ‘The whole internet screams at once’: Downdetector logged 6.4 million U.S. outage reports in a week as Microsoft, the FAA, Chase and Apple went down
items.summary:
Microsoft’s email, the FAA, Chase and Apple all went down within a week. Downdetector, the site people check when an app or website stops working, logged 6.4 million U.S. reports in the seven days ending on Tuesday, four times a typical week, and 14 million worldwide, three times its usual level. The company that runs it thinks the timing is mostly coincidence.

That puts the outage tracker at odds with the explanation taking hold in Washington, where Sen. Mark Warner has blamed organizations racing to patch software flaws that AI tools now find faster than companies can fix them. Downdetector’s data shows big outages getting rarer, and it can’t see what caused any of them. For companies watching their own update queues, the question is whether this week is a blip or the start of something.

Microsoft’s Outlook and Teams went down last week on Nov. 12 and 13, taking out email in more than 70 countries for almost 24 hours. With nearly 3.9 million U.S. reports and 7.8 million worldwide, it was Downdetector’s largest outage since Amazon Web Services went down in October 2025. Then on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country after what it called unstable legacy equipment. Its initial investigation points to two sites, including a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where its network contractor, L3Harris, had been installing a new router. 

And on Monday, a software bug at Chase meant Chase and Wells Fargo customers couldn’t get to their money . Chase drew about 90,000 U.S. reports, roughly 165 times normal and more than twice any other U.S. bank outage this year.…
items.t: ‘The whole internet screams at once’: Downdetector logged 6.4 million U.S. outage reports in a week as Microsoft, the FAA, Chase and Apple went down

items.title: China’s Greater Bay Area was built to rival Silicon Valley. Nearly a decade on, is it finally living up to the hype?
items.summary:
Watch the sunset from Macau, China’s gambling capital, and you’ll see the sun drop behind a cluster of gleaming skyscrapers on an island across a narrow strait.

As recently as 2009, Hengqin—an island in the mainland Chinese city of Zhuhai, just across from Macau—was home to oyster farmers and fishermen. Today the island, three times Macau’s size, is home to an “In-Depth Cooperation Zone,” a development initiative run by Guangdong province and the Macau Special Administrative Region to help the latter diversify its economy away from gambling by tapping mainland talent and manufacturing capacity.

But Hengqin’s multilane highways, striking architecture, and manicured parks haven’t yet brought people with them. In 2009, authorities hoped Hengqin would have 280,000 residents by 2020; by the end of 2025, it had just 50,000.

Hengqin is one test of a much larger integration project: the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macau Greater Bay Area (GBA), which comprises nine cities around the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong province, including Shenzhen, Zhuhai, and Guangzhou, plus the Hong Kong and Macau special administrative regions. Can the GBA turn connectivity and deeper integration into growth?

Pedestrians cross a busy urban road as cars and electric scooters move through traffic beneath a skyline featuring Shun Hing Square, also known as the Diwang Building, KK100 and the Ping An Finance Centre at sunset on August 9, 2026, in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China. Cheng Xin—Getty Images 

The GBA spans three legal systems, currencies, and customs territories. With 88 million people, the…
items.t: China’s Greater Bay Area was built to rival Silicon Valley. Nearly a decade on, is it finally living up to the hype?

items.title: Bill Ackman is asking the wrong question about Nvidia
items.summary:
When an executive leaves suddenly, people watch to see whose calls still get returned. If they believe the old boss might be back in the foreseeable future, they have a reason to wait him out. At Nvidia , where Jensen Huang famously had dozens of direct reports, that ambiguity could reach deep into the business. Bill Ackman thinks Nvidia’s board made a mistake by saying it does not intend to reinstate Huang. I think that statement was one of the more defensible things the board did.

Ackman’s criticism of the original decision deserves a hearing. On Nov. 8, Nvidia announced an independent inquiry and expressed confidence in Huang. On Nov. 11, according to its SEC filing, the board accepted his resignation, effective immediately, and announced his departure the next day. Ackman argues that the directors moved too quickly. Chairman Harvey Jones says Huang resigned voluntarily after disclosing conduct inconsistent with company standards. The board has offered shareholders limited detail about what changed. The speed warrants scrutiny, although the public timeline alone cannot tell us what the directors knew or when they learned it.

But the question of whether the board handled Huang’s departure properly is different from the question of what should happen next. Once he was out, the directors could give interim CEO Colette Kress clear authority or leave employees, customers and prospective successors wondering whether Huang would soon return. Ackman sees the board’s rejection of reinstatement as another failure. A serious and highly qualified candidate for the permanent job…
items.t: Bill Ackman is asking the wrong question about Nvidia

items.title: Social Security has less than 6 years before a 22% cut. A Senate chairman’s fix is to borrow $190 trillion and call it the ‘Stop Scaring Seniors Act’
items.summary:
Social Security’s retirement trust fund is less than six years from running dry, which would trigger an automatic benefit cut of about 22%. Senate Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson has a plan to stop it: Let the Treasury borrow the difference.

On Nov. 18, the Wisconsin Republican put forward a proposal, which the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calls the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. It would let the Treasury Secretary move money from the government’s general fund into the retirement trust fund once its reserves are gone, so beneficiaries would keep getting full checks. CRFB estimates that would add $190 trillion to the national debt over 75 years in inflation-adjusted terms, or 165% of GDP.

For the roughly 70 million people collecting benefits, the cut it would avoid is real money: about $500 a month for the average beneficiary , according to CRFB. The question is who pays instead.

Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget 

“We usually say that inaction is the worst option when it comes to Social Security, but now we found something even worse,” CRFB president Maya MacGuineas said in a statement . She said it was hard to see the bill as anything other than “a cynical pander that ducks all the real decisions we need to confront.”

The bill goes to the bond market 

CRFB, a nonpartisan deficit-hawk group, argues the bigger danger isn’t 75 years out. 

“Even simply passing the legislation could spook the bond market enough to spark financial turmoil,” MacGuineas said, adding the borrowing “would almost certainly spark a crisis.”

The group has run the numbers…
items.t: Social Security has less than 6 years before a 22% cut. A Senate chairman’s fix is to borrow $190 trillion and call it the ‘Stop Scaring Seniors Act’

items.title: Sound Ventures turned $435 million into a $7 billion Anthropic stake. Ashton Kutcher left months before the IPO
items.summary:
When Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude and a suite of large language models and coding tools, went public this morning, the numbers were eye-popping. The San Francisco AI firm raised about $81.3 billion, the most money ever raised in an initial public offering, and began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

Anthropic priced its shares at $83 , above its expected range of $70 to $78. They opened at $111.50 and had cooled to around $98 by mid-afternoon, per Yahoo Finance .

That’s a windfall for Anthropic’s earliest backers, and one of them has a Hollywood pedigree. Sound Ventures , the venture firm co-founded in 2015 by talent manager Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, owns roughly 0.5% of Anthropic, a stake worth about $7 billion , according to Bloomberg.

A new record, and a $1.5 trillion valuation 

For context, the previous record belonged to SpaceX’s June launch, which raised $75 billion. Third, distantly, is South Korean memory-chip maker SK hynix , which raised $26.5 billion in a U.S. listing in July, per Renaissance Capital .

At its IPO price, Anthropic was valued at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis, nearly on par with Meta Platforms and Tesla, worth about $1.58 trillion and $1.52 trillion, respectively, per recent data from The Motley Fool . (SpaceX still holds the record for the richest IPO valuation, at $1.77 trillion, which is why Anthropic’s lower-than-expected pricing drew scrutiny last week.)

That valuation exceeds the GDP of many industrialized nations, including Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and Switzerland, per…
items.t: Sound Ventures turned $435 million into a $7 billion Anthropic stake. Ashton Kutcher left months before the IPO

items.title: ‘Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak’: Harvard economist finds locking up students’ phones adds 1–2 weeks of learning a year
items.summary:
Making students lock their phones in pouches during the school day adds one to two weeks of learning a year, according to a national study released Tuesday.

The study, from Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, with researchers at Dartmouth and the testing nonprofit NWEA, found that schools that required students to store their phones in pouches experienced an annual boost in achievement growth of 0.01 standard deviations—equivalent to one to two weeks of additional learning per year (or restoring two minutes per hour of class time). The team followed 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools across 49 states and Washington, D.C., from the 2021–22 through 2025–26 school years.

The gains are small, but they last. Achievement gains begin in the first year of the ban and appear to continue three years later, and the effect held across elementary, middle and high schools, and across rich and poor ones. 

The result breaks with the last big study of school phone bans, which found in May that they did close to nothing for test scores. The argument has money riding on it: New York and 16 other states put bell-to-bell bans in place last school year, with the cost of a pouch at about $25 a student, according to Tom Kane, an economist and education professor who serves as the director of Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research.

That matters because of how far students have fallen. Kane released an education scorecard that traced a “learning recession” back to 2013, years before the pandemic. Between 2013 and 2024, eighth-grade math and reading achievement fell by…
items.t: ‘Strict cell phone bans seem to plug about half of that leak’: Harvard economist finds locking up students’ phones adds 1–2 weeks of learning a year

items.title: Exclusive: AWS Marketplace head on letting AI agents shop for software: ‘People can’t wait three months to get access to the latest one’
items.summary:
Amazon is rolling out a suite of AI agents to help companies purchase software and procure services on its AWS Marketplace product, including the ability to pre-authorize agents to take certain actions without having to wait for human approval.

Its latest Marketplace update gives people and AI agents tools for each stage of procurement, from finding products and reviewing contract terms to checking vendor security, making purchases and setting up supported software. Companies can give agents a budget to buy certain products and set rules for which purchases go to a person for approval.

Say you ask an AI agent to build a company website. For the login page, many companies choose to select an outside vendor, such as Okta , to set up a sign-in service. The agent can find one that fits, but previously it might have had to wait for someone to approve the purchase before it could deploy and test that vendor’s solution.

“You shouldn’t have to approve that,” Matt Yanchyshyn, vice president of AWS Marketplace and partner services, told Fortune . The product manager who asked for the website to be built may not know which sign-in service to choose. After picking one, the agent should be able to start a free trial and perhaps pay for a month to build a real working prototype on a pay-as-you-go basis, he said.

The way companies shop is already changing. “People aren’t searching with keywords anymore,” Yanchyshyn said, adding that AWS sees the shift in its own metrics. Instead of typing “database,” buyers describe what they want to build and what the software needs to do. An AI…
items.t: Exclusive: AWS Marketplace head on letting AI agents shop for software: “People can’t wait three months to get access to the latest one”

items.title: Target’s turnaround is paying off, with operating profit up 76%, helped by a $301 million tariff windfall
items.summary:
After years of declining sales and dwindling store traffic , Target’s turnaround plan under CEO Michael Fiddelke is showing gains. The retail giant reported $26.45 billion in Q3 merchandise sales for the three months ending Oct. 31, up 6.9% from last year and beating analysts’ expectations of $25.96 billion. Operating profit was $1.67 billion, up 76% from last year and beating analysts’ expectations of $1.3 billion. 

But there’s a wrinkle: $301 million of that profit came from refunds of President Donald Trump’s tariffs, about 18% of the total, according to Target’s Q3 filing released on Nov. 18. Over the first nine months of this year, Target recognized $1.3 billion in tariff refunds following the Supreme Court’s ruling in February that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give the president authority to impose tariffs. 

Still, even without that windfall, Target seems to be recovering. Excluding the $301 million, Target would have reported about $1.37 billion in operating profit, still higher than the $948 million it recorded a year earlier. Neil Saunders, managing director of GlobalData Retail, told Fortune it’s a sign Target is genuinely gaining with consumers. 

“Tariff refunds are certainly very helpful to Target, and they have provided a very nice boost to the bottom line,” Saunders said. “That said, even if you take the tariff gain out, Target is still up on the prior year, and I think that really reflects the fact that the business does have some momentum on the consumer side.” 

He said Target’s investments in revamped stores and new products…
items.t: Target’s turnaround is paying off, with operating profit up 76%, helped by a $301 million tariff windfall

At its $97 closing price, Anthropic’s market cap was just shy of $1.8 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies, alongside giants such as Alphabet , Apple , and Amazon . “This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a statemen t posted on X on Thursday.

items.title: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras
items.summary:
We can’t make AI safe for humanity if tech bosses are allowed to run their companies like autocracies

Over the past two years, a troubling pattern has emerged across the world’s leading AI laboratories. Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As a society we applaud the courage of these individuals and debate their warnings for a news cycle – and then we move on. But we miss the deeper institutional failure those resignations reveal: as the great political scientist Albert Hirschman made clear, exit is not voice.

Isabelle Ferreras is accelerator fellow at the University of Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, FNRS research director at the University of Louvain, Belgium and co-founder of DemocraticIntelligence.org
items.t: When tech workers have to quit their jobs to raise the alarm, it’s time to worry | Isabelle Ferreras

In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’”

Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning, about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours…

He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
items.summary:
It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year

  • Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166

The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January. But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving.

Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use.

items.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares

Thoughts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while, and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down.

Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire. I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company, Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m).

items.title: Hone Health lands $228 million with backing from Jay-Z’s and Gwyneth Paltrow’s firms—and she’s a patient too
items.summary:
When Saad Alam was 35, he told his doctor he was depressed and gaining weight even though he ate well, slept well, and had been an athlete his whole life. The doctor quickly gave him an answer.

“He literally said, ‘Well, South Asian men start to age a little bit early, so let me give you Viagra and an antidepressant,’” Alam told Fortune . “And I was like, ‘That’s complete bullsh-t.’”

So, Alam decided to look for a second opinion. After months of visits to endocrinologists, urologists, and cardiologists, a group of doctors told him he had low testosterone. That led him in 2020 to cofound Hone Health , an online clinic that began by treating men with low testosterone. 

Six years later, Hone announced $228 million in new financing, including a $28 million equity round led by MarcyPen Capital Partners , the investment firm cofounded by Shawn “Jay-Z” Carter, Jay Brown, and Robbie and D’Rita Robinson.

Hone Health’s announcement on Wednesday also discloses that MarcyPen led Hone’s Series A, a role the company had not made public. 

Asked why, Hone said in a statement that MarcyPen “has historically maintained a low public profile, allowing their portfolio companies to remain at the center of their own stories.” Alam told Fortune it’s even simpler for MarcyPen: “Here’s the capital. You guys let the company do all the work, and we want the company to shine—not necessarily everyone that’s surrounding it. They’re quiet on every single one.”

MarcyPen formed in 2024 when Jay-Z’s Marcy Venture Partners merged with Pendulum Holdings’ investment arm.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
